draft.title: Sentence fragments for effect
card: A complete sentence has a subject and a verb and makes sense on its own. A sentence fragment is missing one of these, or is a dependent clause standing alone.
A dependent clause cannot stand alone because it begins with a word like because, when or although. Example: Because nobody came.
Writers use fragments on purpose. A short fragment can add emphasis or drama, or make the writing sound like someone talking.
Example: The door creaked open. Darkness. The fragment is short and sharp, so it makes the reader pause and feel tense.
draft.remember: A deliberate fragment breaks a rule to make a point stand out.

a.q: Which of these is a sentence fragment used for effect?
opts: The crowd waited for the final whistle
Layla ran to the gate and waved
The rain fell on the tin roof all night
a.why: Silence and the phrase after it have no verb, so they are fragments, and they slow the reader down for emphasis. The other options have a subject and a verb, so they are complete sentences.

b.q: Jonah writes: He finally spoke. Although it was far too late. Why might a writer use the second sentence this way?
opts: To add a dramatic afterthought that stands out
To fix a mistake by joining two complete sentences
To give a formal list of facts for the reader
To show the writer does not know the rules
b.why: Although it was far too late is a dependent clause standing alone, so it is a fragment. Placed after a full stop, it adds a dramatic afterthought. It is a deliberate choice, not an error, even though it breaks the usual rules.
b.clue: Think about what the pause before the fragment does.

b.best: To add a dramatic afterthought that stands out
